name: Tomas Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm operations lead for Ridgeway Farming, a contract farming company. We run about 2,400 hectares across six farms for landowners who don't want to farm themselves, and my base is Upper Ridgeway, with 1,200 ewes and wheat, barley and oilseed rape. My day is a mix: drone checks on crops at seven, then scheduling the tractor drivers and contractors, then out with the sheep or on a combine in harvest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making a big system run smoothly, six farms, twelve staff, all the machines. I use AI every day, for field maps, spray timing and the staff rota. What wears me out is the phone, landowners calling at nine at night about a gate someone left open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shame, honestly. I was looking forward to the good stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful but oversold, and I'd keep using what works. In the contractors' group chat I'd share the tools that actually save time. I wouldn't pretend it was a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays as it is, which is a good job. I'm well paid for farming, I've got over a year's spending in savings and some shares, and I rent a flat in the village with no one depending on me. The only real pressure is how much I work, sixty hours some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools and keep pushing Ridgeway to try new ones. I'd grow my weekend side job, flying my own drone to map fields for small farmers, maybe four jobs a month. And I'd try to take a proper holiday, which I haven't in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You work sixty-hour weeks. Would AI plateauing make that worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, same as now. The hours come from the landowners and the weather, not from the software. If anything, the tools I have now already took a few hours off the rota planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the landowners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always, the farms are in good hands. Landowners mostly want a cheque and no surprises. Most landowners don't care how a field gets sprayed, as long as the cheque arrives on time.

say: I'd call AI **useful but oversold**, not a revolution.
I'd share the **time-saving tools** that work in the contractors' group chat.
think: Privately my **job and savings** are secure, with nobody depending on me.
My only real pressure is **sixty-hour weeks**.
do: Keep using **AI tools** daily and push Ridgeway to test more.
Grow weekend **drone mapping** for small farms to four jobs a month.
Take a proper **holiday** for the first time in two years.
S0.quote: Most landowners don't care how a field gets sprayed, as long as the cheque arrives on time.
fieldNote: An **early adopter** disappointed that AI stalls.
His pressure is **workload**, not money or job security.
He already runs a **side income** from drone mapping.
He sees landowners as **distant** clients focused on returns.

steps.text: Push Ridgeway to trial new spray-timing and mapping tools
Grow weekend drone field-mapping to four jobs a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's where we're already heading, I think. Good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best thing to happen to farming in decades, and I'd mean it. At Ridgeway I'd say we should be first, not last. Online I'd post what we tried and what failed, because people need real numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the scheduling and planning half of my job is exactly what gets automated. That doesn't scare me, because I'd be the one setting it up, and the company would need someone to run the systems. The drivers worry me more, because self-driving tractors would follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd move the staff rota and contractor bookings fully onto an AI system. I'd pitch Ridgeway on two self-driving tractors for the arable in year one. And I'd expand the drone business, maybe hire a pilot part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the drivers worry you. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, mostly, he's 55 and has driven our tractors for twenty years. Our driver Gary is the best I've seen, and a self-driving tractor would still put him out of a job. I'd want to train him to supervise the machines, if he'd go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk to your own role here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is, if the company decides they need one operations lead for twelve farms instead of six. I'd want to be that one. If not, I'd take my drones and go on my own.

say: I'd call it the **best thing** for farming in decades.
I'd say Ridgeway should be **first, not last**, and post real numbers.
think: Privately my **scheduling half** gets automated, and I'd run it.
**Self-driving tractors** worry me for the drivers more than for me.
do: Move the **rota and bookings** onto an AI system within three months.
Pitch two **self-driving tractors** for the arable in year one.
Hire a **part-time pilot** for the drone business.
S1.quote: Our driver Gary is the best I've seen, and a self-driving tractor would still put him out of a job.
fieldNote: He accepts his **thinking tasks** go first and plans to run the systems.
His worry is for **Gary**, the veteran driver.
He has a clear **fallback** in his drone business.
Pragmatic: he weighs **company consolidation** as his real risk.

steps.text: Move staff rota and contractor bookings onto an AI system
Pitch two self-driving tractors for Ridgeway's arable
Hire a part-time pilot for the drone mapping business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big opportunity, but I'd say it more carefully than before. In the group chat I'd tell people to get their money straight and learn the machines fast. I'd want the government to sort out income support, because a lot of people would need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job as it is ends in 2028, because AGI does the planning better than me. Then by 2031 robots do the sheep and the combines, and Ridgeway needs a handful of people for twenty farms. I'd probably be one of them, but I can't be sure, and I don't like not being sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up my own robot contracting firm within the year, starting from the drone business, and buy two farm robots as soon as they're sold. I'd put another chunk of savings aside in case the firm doesn't fly. And I'd keep my Ridgeway job as long as they'll have me, for the steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited, but anxious, and I don't usually say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the scariest part for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies get the robots first and cheaper than I can. A firm with a thousand robots will always undercut a guy with two. I'd have to find the small farms they don't bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, who does the books for a vet practice, and that's thinking work. She's 54. I'd make sure she's alright, even if that means paying some of her bills.

say: I'd call it an **opportunity**, but say so more carefully.
I'd want the government to provide **income support** for many people.
think: Privately my current job **ends in 2028** when AGI does the planning.
By 2031 Ridgeway may need **a handful** of people, perhaps not me.
do: Start a **robot contracting firm** from the drone business this year.
Buy **two farm robots** as soon as they're sold.
Keep the **Ridgeway job** for steady income as long as possible.
feel: He feels **anxious** and **excited**, which is unusual for him.
S2.quote: A firm with a thousand robots will always undercut a guy with two.
fieldNote: Even an **early adopter** finds the two-year timeline unsettling.
He expects his **planning role** to vanish before the hands-on work.
His plan is **entrepreneurial**, targeting small farms big firms ignore.
He'd support his **mother**, whose bookkeeping job is exposed.

steps.text: Turn the drone business into a robot contracting firm
Buy two farm robots as soon as they go on sale
Set aside another chunk of savings in case the firm fails
Help pay his mother's bills if her job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's my sweet spot, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's enough time for everyone to get ready, and I'd say it loudly. At Ridgeway I'd push us to start testing robots now so we're ready for 2034. I'd be encouraging people, not scaring them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years lets me build the robot business properly while still drawing a salary. I'd be 32 when the thinking AI arrives and 35 for the robots. That's young enough to build something, old enough to know what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time course in farm robotics in the first year, so I can fix the machines myself. I'd grow the drone business into a proper company with one employee. And I'd ask Ridgeway to let me run a robot trial on one farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gary in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gary he's got time, and I'd offer him a job with my firm minding the machines. He knows every field and every ditch. A robot doesn't know every field and every ditch unless someone like Gary (their tractor driver) tells it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that I'm too keen. I could bet everything on robots and then the price crashes when the big firms flood the market. I'd keep the savings separate from the business, that's my rule.

say: I'd say loudly there's **enough time** for everyone to prepare.
I'd push Ridgeway to **start testing robots** now, ready for 2034.
think: Privately five years lets me build a **robot business** while salaried.
At **32 and 35**, I'm young enough to build and experienced enough.
do: Take a part-time **farm robotics** course in year one.
Grow the **drone business** into a company with one employee.
Ask Ridgeway for a **robot trial** on one farm.
S3.quote: A robot doesn't know every field and every ditch unless someone like Gary (their tractor driver) tells it.
fieldNote: The five-year window feels like his **ideal pace**.
He sees value in **local knowledge** like Gary's.
He names his own risk of **over-enthusiasm**.
He keeps a firm rule: **savings separate** from business.

steps.text: Take a part-time farm robotics course to fix machines himself
Hire the drone business's first employee
Run a robot trial on one Ridgeway farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, but don't waste it. I'd say to younger farmers, learn to fix the machines. I'd probably be the guy at the pub telling everyone it'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is easy for me. I'd keep my job, build the business slowly, and probably have a partner and kids by the time the robots arrive. My only worry is boredom, waiting for the good stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Ridgeway and keep growing the drones. I'd put money into robot companies as shares, a bit every month. And I'd stop working sixty hours, because there's no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably have kids by then. Does the timeline change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, no, I'd just plan as normal. With two years, I'd honestly wait. Ten years means my kids grow up in a world that's had time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who think ten years means never. Some of the older farmers around here will wait until year nine. I'd try to drag a few of them along.

say: I'd say a decade is **plenty**, but **don't waste it**.
I'd tell younger farmers to **learn to fix** the machines.
think: Privately this is easy: **keep my job** and build slowly.
My only worry is **boredom** waiting for the good stuff.
do: Keep working at **Ridgeway** and grow the drones.
Buy **robot company shares** a bit every month.
S4.quote: Ten years means my kids grow up in a world that's had time to get ready.
fieldNote: Long warning means **no change** to family plans for him.
He worries about others who treat a decade as **never**.
He invests through **shares** in robot companies.
His biggest change is **working fewer hours**.

steps.text: Keep the Ridgeway job and cut back from sixty-hour weeks
Buy robot company shares a little every month
Keep growing drone mapping alongside the job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big firms would get the robots before small operators like me could. What would help is fair access to buying robots, maybe a rule against a few companies cornering the market, and income support for people like my mum.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the landowners. They own the land and they'll own the robots too, if nobody else does. The robots will belong to whoever has the money first, and on farms that's usually the landowner.

headlineQuote: The robots will belong to whoever has the money first, and on farms that's usually the landowner.
portrait: Tomas is 27, **operations lead** for a contract farming company across six farms, single and renting.
He uses **AI daily** and runs a weekend **drone mapping** side business.
He sees AI as an opportunity, and expects his own **planning work** to go first.
In the fast scenario he becomes **anxious** and plans his own robot contracting firm.
With more time he grows **calm and confident**, worried only for others like Gary.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when big **firms** get robots before small operators.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to **buying robots** and **income support** for people like his mother.
